entries.title: ¿Crees en los White Sox? La confianza del equipo está creciendo, y más tras la victoria ante  los Cubs
entries.summary: <p>El receptor Edgar Quero recordó haber dicho durante el entrenamiento de primavera que los White Sox tienen un equipo realmente bueno.</p><p>Sonaba bonito, pero tal vez no era realista. Habían perdido al menos 100 juegos en tres temporadas consecutivas y parecían estar a años de ser decentes, no se diga realmente buenos.</p><p>Quizás Quero sabía algo que el resto del mundo del béisbol no sabía. O tal vez él y los Sox estaban simulando hasta lograrlo.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0c0000" name="module-0c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>De cualquier manera, casi dos meses en la temporada, los Sox lucen sólidos. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/edgar-quero-white-sox-rally-past-cubs-to-take-crosstown-series" target="_blank" >El jonrón de dos carreras de Quero en la décima entrada</a> el domingo le dio a los Sox una victoria de 9-8 sobre los Cubs. Ante una multitud bulliciosa y dividida de 38,608 personas, los Sox completaron una racha de 7-2 en casa, el mejor de al menos nueve juegos desde una racha de 8-2 a finales de junio y principios de julio de 2008.</p><p>“Significa mucho para todos en el equipo”, dijo Quero. “Significa mucho ganar esta serie. Significa mucho para todos, especialmente porque estamos jugando un béisbol realmente bueno. Estoy feliz por este equipo”.</p><p>Los Sox no han tenido mucho de qué alegrarse durante años. Son una franquicia en medio de su segunda gran reconstrucción en una década, y se esperaba poco de ellos en 2026, aparte de algún avance.</p><p>Pero esta serie en casa mostró que podrían estar adelantados a lo previsto. En los nueve juegos, demostraron que pueden ganar de varias maneras. Estuvo la tensa victoria de 2-1 el domingo pasado contra los Mariners, la barrida a los Royals, en la que los Sox anotaron seis carreras en cada juego, y la exhibición de poder del sábado, cuando conectaron cinco jonrones.</p><p>Luego estuvo la resiliencia que mostraron el domingo, cuando iban abajo 3-0 y 4-1, pero se mantuvieron en el juego.</p><p>“Han continuado jugando los nueve innings, cada lanzamiento”, comentó el mánager Will Venable.</p><p>Que la racha de los Sox terminara con una victoria en la serie contra los Cubs —su primera desde 2022— les da más impulso antes de dirigirse al oeste para jugar contra los Mariners y los Giants.</p><p>“Obviamente, la rivalidad es algo grande”, dijo Tristan Peters, cuyo jonrón de tres carreras en la octava entrada le dio a los Sox una ventaja de 7-4. “Sabemos que son un buen equipo, pero también creemos que somos un equipo realmente bueno. Y acabamos de demostrarlo”.</p><p>Los Sox claramente no son perfectos. Si van a competir en la Liga Americana, necesitarán ayudar al bullpen, que les perjudicó el domingo cuando Seranthony Domínguez permitió el jonrón del empate de tres carreras de Michael Conforto en la novena.</p><p>A pesar del surgimiento de Davis Martin, la rotación podría requerir al menos otro brazo probado. Y no hay pruebas de que la alineación pueda seguir produciendo como lo ha hecho durante toda una temporada, quizás bajo la presión de una carrera por los playoffs cuando cada turno al bate se vuelve más intenso.</p><p>Sin embargo, como destacó la serie en casa, los Sox han ganado confianza. Y aunque no hagan una carrera, las cosas se sienten mucho mejor de lo que han estado recientemente. Los Sox parecen una franquicia que va por la dirección correcta después de años de quemar buena voluntad con los aficionados.</p><p>Las victorias también se sienten legítimas. Estos Sox no tienen que decirse a sí mismos que son capaces de ganar ni convencer a los escépticos.</p><p>“Estamos trayendo a las personas adecuadas; tenemos un gran liderazgo con nuestro cuerpo técnico; tenemos grandes compañeros de equipo”, dijo el campocorto Colson Montgomery. “Lo de ‘simula hasta lograrlo’ puede ser cierto y puede ser contagioso. Una vez que comienzas a ganar, es como, ‘Está bien, esto es real, no es falso’. Creo que lo que tenemos aquí es real”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
entries.author: Brian Sandalow

entries.title: Severe weather causing delays at airports as thunderstorms move through Chicago area
entries.summary: <p>A severe thunderstorm watch has been issued by the National Weather Service for the Chicago area, causing some delays and cancellations at O'Hare and Midway airports, officials said. </p><p>The watch, in effect until 5 p.m., covers portions of Illinois and Indiana, including Chicago and Cook County, according to a statement from the city's Office of Emergency Management and Communications. </p><p>The stormy situation is causing some delays at Chicago's airports, according to the FAA. </p><p>Some flights arriving at O'Hare International Airport could be delayed an average of one hour and 15 minutes, the FAA said. </p><p>But generally, O'Hare is averaging delays of 42 minutes, with 11 cancellations, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.flychicago.com/business/media/delays/pages/default.aspx" target="_blank" >FlyChicago.com. </a>At Midway Airport, delays are averaging about 25 minutes with a single cancellation. </p><p>The hazardous outlook includes a slight chance large, quarter-sized hail and wind gusts of up to 60 miles per hour, according to the National Weather Service. </p><p>As of midday, it was breezy, overcast and about 69 degrees at Midway, and showers are likely to continue through the afternoon. </p><p>Thunderstorms can happen suddenly and can include flash floods, damaging winds, tornados, or dangerous lightning, the statement said, adding it is important to be prepared, take shelter and stay informed. </p><p>Keep in mind outdoor sirens are intended for those outdoors to seek shelter, the statement said. </p><p>The city also urges motorists to use caution and avoid driving through standing water on streets, viaducts and low-lying areas. Residents can visit <a class="Link" href="http://311.chicago.gov/" target="_blank" >311.chicago.gov</a>, use the CHI311 app or dial 3-1-1 to report any tree emergency, water in basements, standing water in the street, or viaduct flooding.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Ordenan el cierre de Ford City Mall para antes del 22 de junio
entries.summary: <p>El deteriorado Ford City Mall, ubicado en el suroeste de Chicago, debe cerrar antes del mediodía del 22 de junio, informaron funcionarios municipales el viernes.</p><p>La fecha de cierre fue anunciada durante una breve audiencia judicial. Se esperaba que el juez de circuito Leonard Murray firmara la orden de cierre en respuesta a la solicitud de los funcionarios de la Ciudad de Chicago, quienes señalaron <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/20/ford-city-mall-esta-a-punto-de-cerrar-tras-falta-de-reparaciones" target="_blank" >el deterioro</a> de la propiedad como un "peligro inminente" para los inquilinos y compradores. La Municipalidad ha destacado como peligros las inundaciones, el cableado expuesto y los posibles agujeros en el suelo.</p><p>La orden afectaría a aproximadamente dos docenas de minoristas, incluyendo el último inquilino ancla del centro comercial, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2026/04/24/jcpenney-retrocede-de-su-cierre-en-ford-city-pero-el-centro-comercial-sigue-en-peligro" target="_blank" >JCPenney</a>. Otras tiendas mencionadas en el borrador de la orden incluyen Foot Locker, Sam's Furniture y Victoria's Secret. Muchos comerciantes ya han abandonado el centro comercial.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7b0000" name="module-7b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Greg Janes, abogado asistente de la Municipalidad, declaró en la audiencia que todas las partes en el caso han acordado el cierre del 22 de junio.</p><p>El cierre forzado ocurre tras años de declive de las ventas en el centro comercial, ubicado en 7601 S. Cicero Ave. Su propietario es Namdar Realty Group, una firma con sede en Great Neck, Nueva York, especializada en propiedades en dificultades.</p><p>La orden no afecta al cine cercano, a edificios anexos ni a una sección al norte del centro comercial principal que incluye Planet Fitness. Namdar estaba obligado a mantener un sistema de supresión de incendios que sirve a esas propiedades.</p><p>El concejal Derrick Curtis, cuyo 18.º distrito incluye el centro comercial, ha acusado a Namdar de permitir que la propiedad se deteriorara y de no hacer nada para detener las ocupaciones "derivadas" de su estacionamiento, donde los conductores giran sus autos ruidosamente.</p><p>"Hemos estado pidiendo seguridad en el lugar durante años", dijo Curtis. Llamó la decisión del juez "una gran victoria" que podría impulsar la reurbanización del lote de aproximadamente 60 acres, donde Dodge fabricó motores de aeronaves durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial y Ford hizo lo mismo en la Guerra de Corea.</p><p>Un promotor inmobiliario mantuvo el nombre de Ford para presentar el sitio como un centro comercial en 1965. Hace mucho tiempo contaba con un Carson Pirie Scott y un Sears como anclas.</p><p>Curtis ha informado a sus votantes de que Kurv Industrial quiere reemplazar el centro comercial por almacenes o por manufactura ligera. "Espero poder hablar con ellos muy pronto porque esta es una pieza importante de la comunidad", dijo.</p><p>Namdar no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>JCPenney dijo en un correo electrónico: "A pesar de nuestros mejores esfuerzos por permanecer en Ford City Mall, JCPenney cerrará esta ubicación al público el 21 de junio de 2026, como resultado de la moción de la Ciudad de Chicago para desalojar la propiedad debido a preocupaciones de seguridad no atendidas por el propietario. Estamos explorando activamente oportunidades para una nueva ubicación de la tienda en el área circundante de Chicago".</p><p>El minorista también tiene una tienda en Chicago Ridge Mall, en 95th Street y Ridgeland Avenue.</p><p>Otra audiencia en el caso de Ford City está programada para el 29 de junio.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
entries.author: David Roeder

entries.title: DraftKings pulls plug on in-person betting at Wrigley Field
entries.summary: <p>After a tough weekend on the South Side, Cubs fans now have to deal with losing in-person betting at the DraftKings Sportsbook at Wrigley Field.</p><p>The company blames Illinois’ high taxes on sports wagering as the reason for its decision, saying in-person betting will end May 31.</p><p>The nearly three-year-old venue, adjacent to Wrigley Field, will still remain open as a restaurant. Currently, it’s the only <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2020/9/3/21419992/cubs-looking-to-open-mlbs-first-sportsbook-at-wrigley-field-draftkings-chicago-illinois" >retail sportsbook in Illinois</a> connected to a sports venue.</p><p>"While we are proud of what we have built alongside the Chicago Cubs, we are taking a more focused approach to where we invest in the state. The cost of operating in Illinois, including its high tax structure, makes it more difficult to justify continued investment in a standalone retail sportsbook. We remain committed to serving our mobile sportsbook customers,” DraftKings said in a statement.</p><p>Illinois ranks fifth in the U.S. for highest sports betting taxes and is number one in the Midwest, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoispolicy.org/illinois-sports-betting-taxes-5th-highest-in-nation-highest-in-midwest/" target="_blank" >Illinois Policy Institute</a>.</p><p>When sports betting became legal in Illinois in 2019, sportsbooks paid a flat 15% tax on revenue earned. Illinois lawmakers have since raised the tax to as high as 40%, according to the institute. Last year, the state added a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2025/06/10/sports-betting-tax-illinois-fanduel-draftkings-general-assembly-budget" >per-wager tax</a> of 25 cents on the first 20 million wagers per year, then 50 cents for every bet beyond that.</p><p>“It [high taxes] does pose a challenge in having to pass it on to consumers,” Parker Winslow, senior manager of corporate communications at DraftKings, said. “Having to pass that cost onto consumers generally makes the legal industry less appealing and sends customers to illegal markets.”</p><p>Winslow said DraftKings will continue to operate its online sportsbooks across the state.</p><p>He said the decision to end in-person betting at Wrigley Field means laying off about two dozen employees.</p><p>The Cubs said in a statement that the DraftKings bar and restaurant will remain open.</p><p>“Later this season, we expect to create a seamless flow between the bar and the ballpark concourse, making the space a great gameday option for Cubs ticketholders. DraftKings has been a great partner and will continue to be the Official Sports Betting and Daily Fantasy Partner of the Chicago Cubs,” the Cubs said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/12/30/chicago-sports-betting-tax-lawsuit-tro-draftkings-fanduel" >FanDuel, DraftKings, other big sportsbooks sue to block new Chicago sports betting tax</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Michael Puente | WBEZ

entries.title: Cook County prosecutors launch new task force to address violent crime on public transit
entries.summary: <p>The Cook County state’s attorney’s office announced a new task force Monday that will bring together officials from a swath of local, state and federal agencies to discuss how to improve safety on public transit.</p><p>The group will convene monthly to analyze violent incidents that have happened on or near public transit systems and work to bring charges.</p><p>“The task force mission is clear: promote public safety on transit systems by working in collaboration together,” Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke said at a news conference.</p><p>The task force will include representatives from Metra; Pace; the Chicago Transit Authority; the Chicago Police Department; the Cook County sheriff’s office; the U.S. attorney’s office; the Federal Bureau of Investigation; the Drug Enforcement Administration; and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.</p><p>Two months into a security surge, CTA leadership boasted last week that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/13/cta-violent-crime-nora-leerhsen" target="_blank" >violent crime was decreasing</a> on the transit system. However, a Sun-Times analysis found serious attacks <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/02/chicago-cta-transit-crime-assault-battery-leerhsen" target="_blank" >remained historically high</a>.</p><p>On Monday, O’Neill Burke touted that violent crime on public transportation had dropped by 22% compared to May of last year.</p><p>“But that is not good enough,” O’Neill Burke told reporters. “This is not a job accomplished moment. In order to make this system as safe as possible, we need to continue to expand our work, so that everyone feels safe on public transit.”</p><p>The regional transit task force builds on the internal transit crime task force her office unveiled in March to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/25/oneill-burke-transit-task-force-cook-cta-crime-prosecution" target="_blank" >bolster prosecutions</a> of crime on the CTA.</p><p>That task force set out to train more than 30 prosecutors on how to track data on transit crimes, review CTA video evidence, and serve as liaisons with Chicago police and CTA on transit-related cases.</p><p>“That was so successful that we said we need to expand this to the entire region, and that's where the regional transit task force came from,” O’Neill Burke said.</p><p>The regional transit task force is set to meet for the first time next week.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/13/cta-violent-crime-nora-leerhsen" target="_blank" >CTA touts drop in serious crime 2 months into security surge — but violent attacks remain at historic high</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/02/chicago-cta-transit-crime-assault-battery-leerhsen" target="_blank" >Violent attacks surge on CTA as Trump threatens $50 million funding cut over transit crime</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/10/chicago-transit-authority-cta-crime-security-plan-fta" target="_blank" >CTA’s new security plan includes sheriff’s deputies on trains, high-barrier gates and farecard inspections</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Anna Savchenko | WBEZ

entries.title: Universidad de Chicago ofrecerá colegiatura gratuita para estudiantes de familias que ganen menos de $250,000 al año
entries.summary: <p>La Universidad de Chicago se une a otras universidades de élite al ofrecer matrícula gratis a estudiantes cuyas familias ganan menos de $250,000 al año, anunció la escuela el miércoles como parte de una iniciativa para hacer la universidad accesible para familias de clase media y clase media alta.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://news.uchicago.edu/story/uchicago-will-offer-free-tuition-families-incomes-below-250000-greatly-expanding" target="_blank" >A partir del otoño de 2027</a>, los estudiantes cuyas familias ganen menos de $250,000 al año podrán asistir sin costo de colegiatura, y los estudiantes cuyas familias ganen menos de $125,000 al año también recibirán alojamiento gratuito, comidas y la exoneración de otras tarifas. La oferta está destinada a familias con activos "típicos", que pueden incluir ahorros modestos y una vivienda propia.</p><p>El costo de asistencia en la Universidad de Chicago para estudiantes de pregrado se aproxima a los $100,000 al año. El costo total de este año escolar de colegiatura, alojamiento y otras tarifas fue de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/08/31/college-university-tuition-costs-fees-illinois-uic-education-northwestern-loyola" target="_blank" >$98,300, un aumento del 3.5% comparado al año anterior.</a> La matrícula sola rondó los $71,000.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-080000" name="module-080000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“La Universidad de Chicago se enorgullece de patrocinar un ambiente de aprendizaje caracterizado por la curiosidad intelectual, la ambición y el rigor”, dijo el presidente de la Universidad, Paul Alivisatos, en un comunicado de prensa. “Al profundizar nuestro compromiso con la accesibilidad, estamos ayudando a garantizar que las mentes más brillantes puedan unirse a nosotros”.</p><p>El estudiante promedio de pregrado en la Universidad de Chicago recibe alrededor de $75,000 en ayuda financiera, según el comunicado. En total, la universidad distribuye aproximadamente $225 millones anuales en ayudas.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/article/which-colleges-offer-free-tuition.html" target="_blank" >Otras universidades prestigiosas han tomado pasos similares</a> para hacer que la educación superior sea más accesible y aliviar la carga de costos para los estudiantes y sus familias. En los últimos años, escuelas como <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/03/17/nx-s1-5330842/harvard-admission-tuition-free-affirmative-action" target="_blank" >la Universidad Harvard</a>, la Universidad Columbia y el <a class="Link" href="https://news.mit.edu/2024/mit-tuition-undergraduates-family-income-1120" target="_blank" >Instituto Tecnológico de Massachusetts</a> han exonerado de las tarifas de colegiatura para estudiantes cuyas familias ingresan menos de cierta cantidad, típicamente entre $150,000 y $200,000 al año.</p><p>En el área de Chicago, la Universidad Northwestern ofrece colegiatura gratuita a la mayoría de los estudiantes de familias que ganan menos de $150,000 al año, y la mayoría de los estudiantes cuyas familias tienen un ingreso inferior a $70,000 al año asisten a la escuela sin costo alguno.</p><p>El anuncio es el más reciente en una serie de pasos para expandir el acceso a la Universidad de Chicago en los últimos años.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://promise.uchicago.edu/index.html" target="_blank" >El programa UChicago Promise</a>, por ejemplo, ofrece becas de colegiatura completa a ciertos graduados de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) y de los City Colleges of Chicago. Los hijos de educadores de CPS y de policías y bomberos de Chicago también son elegibles para becas de colegiatura completa bajo el programa.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>
entries.author: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Services announced for veteran Chicago firefighter who died during training exercise in West Ridge
entries.summary: <p>Services have been announced for veteran Chicago Firefighter Steven M. Decker, who died last week during training, officials said. </p><p>Visitation for Steven M. Decker, 61, will be held Thursday from 2 p.m. - 8 p.m. at Colonial-Wojciechowski Funeral Homes of Chicago, 6250 N. Milwaukee Ave., fire officials said.</p><p>Decker's funeral will be Friday at 10 a.m. at St. Paul Lutheran Church 5650 N. Canfield Ave. in Chicago. </p><p>Decker was injured Thursday afternoon during a training exercise in the 6600 block of North Kedzie Avenue and was taken to Saint Francis Hospital in Evanston, Chicago Fire Department officials said. </p><p>Decker had been with the Chicago Fire Department for nearly 30 years and was an engineer on Engine Company 71, according to Chicago Fire Fighters Union Local 2. That company is stationed at 6239 N. California Ave. in West Ridge. </p><p>Engine Company 71 is located in the 50th Ward, which is also where the training exercise was being conducted. That ward is represented by Ald. Debra Silverstein, who offered her “deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, and fellow first responders” in a statement on social media.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Illinois resident suspected of having hantavirus tests negative for illness
entries.summary: <p>An Illinois resident who was tested for hantavirus does not have the infection, state health officials said Monday. </p><p>The Winnebago County resident <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/12/hantavirus-illinois" target="_blank" >was tested last week</a> after they were likely exposed to rodent droppings and developed mild symptoms that did not require hospitalization, the Illinois Department of Public Health said at the time. The person did not come into contact within anyone tied to the cruise ship hantavirus outbreak that made headlines in recent weeks.</p><p>The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tested the patient and did not detect hantavirus, according to the state health department. Health officials stressed that the risk for the virus spreading in Illinois remains very low. </p><p>Three people <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/hantavirus-outbreak-hondius-cruise-ship-df0e7e1fb9c7fd3e4092be06e684f644" target="_blank" >died from the hantavirus outbreak</a> on the cruise ship MV Hondius that set off April 1 from Argentina. Nine confirmed cases have been linked to that outbreak. Symptoms can include fever, chills and muscle aches, and usually show between one to eight weeks after exposure.</p><p>None of those cruise ship passengers were from Illinois, according to the Illinois and Chicago departments of public health.</p><p>The state has had seven cases of hantavirus since 1993, the most recent being in March 2025, according to the state agency.</p>
entries.author: Kaitlin Washburn

entries.title: Ford City Mall on Southwest Side ordered to close by June 22
entries.summary: <p>The flagging Ford City Mall on Chicago’s Southwest Side must close by noon on June 22, city officials said Friday.</p><p>The closing date was announced during a brief court hearing. Circuit Judge Leonard Murray was expected to sign the closing order in response to city officials <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/17/ford-city-mall-verge-shuttering-namdar-failure-repairs" >citing decay</a> at the property as an “imminent danger” to tenants and shoppers. The city has listed flooding, exposed wiring and potential sinkholes as hazards.</p><p>The order would affect about two dozen retailers, including the mall’s last anchor tenant, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/24/jcpenney-backtracks-ford-city-shutdown-mall-peril" >JCPenney</a>. Other stores listed in the draft order include Foot Locker, Sam’s Furniture and Victoria’s Secret. Many merchants already have left the mall.</p><p>Greg Janes, assistant corporation counsel for the city, said at the hearing that all parties in the case have agreed to the June 22 shutdown.</p><p>The forced closure comes after years of declining sales at the mall, 7601 S. Cicero Ave. Its owner is Namdar Realty Group, a Great Neck, New York-based firm that specializes in distressed property.</p><p>The order doesn't affect a nearby movie theater, outbuildings and a section north of the main mall that includes Planet Fitness. Namdar was required to maintain a fire suppression system that serves those properties.</p><p>Ald. Derrick Curtis, whose 18th Ward includes the mall, has accused Namdar of letting the property slide and doing nothing to stop “drifting” takeovers of its parking lot, where drivers loudly spin their tires.</p><p>“We’ve been asking for security on the grounds there for years,” Curtis said. He called the judge’s decision “a huge win” that could spur redevelopment of the roughly 60-acre parcel, where Dodge built aircraft engines in World War II and Ford did the same in the Korean War. </p><p>A developer kept the Ford name to introduce the site as a mall in 1965. It long ago boasted a Carson Pirie Scott and Sears as anchors.</p><p>Curtis has told constituents that Kurv Industrial wants to replace the mall with warehouses or light manufacturing. “I’m hoping to talk with them very soon because this is an important piece of the community,” he said.</p><p>Namdar didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>JCPenney said in an email, “Despite our best efforts to remain at Ford City Mall, JCPenney will close this location to the public by June 21, 2026, as a result of the city of Chicago’s motion to vacate the property due to safety concerns not addressed by the landlord. We are actively exploring opportunities for a new store location in the surrounding Chicago area.”</p><p></p><p>Another hearing in the Ford City case was scheduled for June 29.</p><p><i>This story has been updated to remove the mention of JCPenney at Chicago Ridge Mall. The retailer doesn't have a location at the center.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/07/16/ford-city-mall-losing-shoppers-bridge-industrial-evolution" >Ford City Mall, losing its hold on shoppers, could see an industrial evolution</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: David Roeder

entries.title: Bears to update NFL on stadium sites — and Chicago isn't one of them
entries.summary: <p>Despite Mayor Brandon Johnson’s top adviser insisting Friday there’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/15/mayor-brandon-johnson-aide-jason-lee-chicago-bears-stadium-arlington-heights-northwest-indiana-lakefront-site" target="_blank" >still a chance</a> the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> build a stadium in the city, the team still considers Arlington Heights and Hammond, Indiana, the only two viable sites.</p><p>The Bears will reiterate that point Tuesday when they update the 31 other NFL teams on the status of the Arlington Heights and Hammond sites — and nowhere else. The briefing will take place at the NFL’s quarterly meeting in Orlando, a source said Monday.</p><p>The Bears updated the NFL Stadium Committee on the two sites in a virtual meeting three weeks ago. Then, as is the case now, the Bears stressed that Arlington Heights and Hammond were the only two realistic locations for their domed stadium.</p><p>The team has said it plans to decide between the two in late spring or early summer.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/18/gov-jb-pritzker-mayor-brandon-johnson-bears-stadium-chicago-arlington-heights-northwest-indiana" >Gov. Pritzker says Mayor Johnson has ‘no plan’ to keep the Bears in Chicago</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The Illinois General Assembly is set to adjourn at the end of the month, so the clock is ticking for the Senate to pass the mega-projects bill that would allow the Bears to negotiate a property tax break with Arlington Heights. The team owns the 326-acre former Arlington International Racecourse site.</p><p>Indiana has proposed building a stadium for the Bears near Wolf Lake and allowing the team to keep all event revenue. The Bears wouldn’t have to pay rent for at least 30 years and could buy back the stadium for a $1 after 40.</p><p>On Friday, senior mayoral adviser Jason Lee shot holes in both plans and told the Sun-Times that “there’s always the realistic possibility that you have to make a pivot” back to the city of Chicago. Monday, Gov. J.B. Pritzker said that Johnson has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/18/gov-jb-pritzker-mayor-brandon-johnson-bears-stadium-chicago-arlington-heights-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" >“come up with no plan at all”</a> to keep the Bears in the city.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8e0000" name="module-8e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Latest on the Bears stadium </h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/11/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana-what-to-know" ><b>Arlington Heights or Hammond</b></a>: The Bears no longer want to play in the smallest stadium in the NFL, so they’re on the hunt for a new place to play. They appear to be down to two options — Arlington Heights, where they purchased the old horse racetrack, or Hammond, Indiana, where lawmakers are making an aggressive push to lure the Bears over the state line. Mitchell Armentrout breaks down the key differences between the two options. <br><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/07/mayor-brandon-johnson-springfield-trip-bears-stadium-arlington-heights-city-revenues" ><b>Johnson still wants to block a move</b></a>: During a recent visit to Springfield, Mayor Brandon Johnson made clear he’s still unhappy about the Bears’ likely departure from the city. It’s unclear how he could stop it from happening, though.<br><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/01/bears-president-kevin-warren-targets-late-spring-or-early-summer-for-stadium-decision" ><b>Decision timeline</b></a>: Bears president Kevin Warren said in early April the team aimed to make a final decision by late spring or early summer.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago History Museum violated law after firing employees for unionizing, federal labor board alleges
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago History Museum violated federal labor laws after management disciplined and fired employees for unionizing last year, the National Labor Relations Board alleges in a complaint filed last week. </p><p>The NLRB says the museum's former president and former human resources chief started retaliating against employees after they voted to form a union last April, according to a news release from the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 31, the union representing museum employees.</p><p>In response, AFSCME Council 31 filed five charges against the museum. Roughly a year later, the NLRB Chicago office issued its formal complaint against the museum — a rare step given that the board only issues such complaints in 3% of unfair labor practice cases each year, according to AFSCME. </p><p>“It’s illegal to retaliate against workers for exercising their freedom to form a union,” AFSCME Council 31 Executive Director Roberta Lynch said. “Although these actions occurred under previous museum leadership, the organization is responsible for that conduct and must make it right.”</p><p>A spokesperson for the Chicago History Museum did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Museum employees voted to unionize on April 1, 2025. Immediately after, Shatierra Parks, the former HR chief, fired four employees, disciplined four others and threatened all employees with termination because of the union effort, according to the NLRB complaint. </p><p>Later that month, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2025/04/23/chicago-history-museum-union-management-retaliation-firing" target="_blank" >employees wrote a letter</a> to the museum’s board of trustees alleging that management retaliated against employees for organizing. </p><p>But nothing changed, according to the complaint. Three employees were disciplined in May. And in July the museum's former President Donald Lassere laid off two employees and converted four employees from full-time work to part-time.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/01/07/chicago-history-museum-president-out-donald-e-lassere" target="_blank" >Lassere stepped down in January</a> after serving in the role for nearly five years, prompting calls from community members for leadership to reverse the cuts to staff. It's not clear when Parks departed her post. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/01/30/chicago-history-museum-ceo-abakanowicz-research-center-city-architecture" >Community members warn that Chicago History Museum cuts could impact scholarship of city history</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Management fired, disciplined and demoted employees because the "employees formed and assisted the Union and engaged in concerted activities, and to discourage employees from engaging in these activities,” the NLRB complaint reads. That conduct means the museum violated the rights workers are guaranteed under the National Labor Relations Act.</p><p>The museum must respond to the complaint by May 29. </p><p>Read the full complaint:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/25/4a/d66dd51b4ccc8fd3d4caf203bca3/cpt-13-ca-363408-complaint-and-notice-of-hearing.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Gov. Pritzker says Mayor Johnson has 'no plan' to keep the Bears in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson has “no plan” to keep the Bears in Chicago, Gov. JB Pritzker said Monday, declaring Johnson's long-shot hope for city control over the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority “typical” for a mayor he says has accomplished little in Springfield.</p><p>The governor’s remarks about the way the rookie mayor does business with the Illinois General Assembly revive early tensions between Pritzker and Johnson that the two men had seemingly tried to downplay in recent months.</p><p>“He has no plan. He’s come up with no plan at all about how the Bears would end up in the city of Chicago. So that’s problematic. I’d love them to be in the city, but we are three years in now, and he still has no plan,” Pritzker told reporters at an unrelated event in Chicago. “This is kind of typical in fact. ... The mayor has shown up every spring at the end of session to pronounce what he would like to see happen.”</p><p>Pritzker’s claim that Johnson has no plan to keep the Bears in Chicago is not quite accurate. Two years ago, Johnson joined Bears president Kevin Warren in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/04/23/bears-new-stadium-dome-lakefront-soldier-field" >unveiling plans</a> for a domed lakefront stadium adjacent to Soldier Field that would have required $2.4 billion in public support.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/24/bears-stadium-bill-jb-pritzker-illinois-senate" target="_blank" >Pritzker</a> and Democratic legislative leaders were conspicuously absent. The mayor’s plan went nowhere in Springfield. Since then, Chicago has been missing in action from stadium negotiations — until early May, when Johnson made a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/07/mayor-brandon-johnson-springfield-trip-bears-stadium-arlington-heights-city-revenues" target="_blank" > two-day trip</a> to Springfield to, among other things, attempt to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/05/mayor-brandon-johnson-bears-stadium-legislation-arlington-heights-kam-buckner" target="_blank" >tank the Bears’ move</a> to Arlington Heights.</p><p>On Monday, Pritzker conducted an abbreviated tutorial — for reporters and for the Johnson administration — about how Springfield does business.</p><p>The state budget “gets put together starting in November” and is introduced by the governor in February, Pritzker said.</p><p>“That seems like a good time period to come talk to the governor’s office. Then there is February to May. There is all that time to come talk to the Legislature, which has my budget in hand, or the governor’s office,” Pritzker said. “Again, we’ve seen almost nothing out of the mayoral administration here — on that subject or really any other. So to show up in May and have a bunch of demands seems late in the game. And it’s unfortunate that this has happened most years.”</p><p>Last week, Johnson touted to Crain’s Chicago Business the possibility that the city could take control of the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority, created in 1987 as a funding mechanism for the construction of Rate Field where the White Sox play, and the 2003 renovation of Soldier Field.</p><p>That would give the city new clout in the wrangling over a new Bears stadium, but it’s unlikely control of the authority would change hands anytime soon. The governor appoints four members of the seven-member authority's board, while the mayor appoints three.</p><p>The following day, senior mayoral adviser<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/15/mayor-brandon-johnson-aide-jason-lee-chicago-bears-stadium-arlington-heights-northwest-indiana-lakefront-site" > Jason Lee insisted</a> to the Chicago Sun-Times that there’s still a chance to keep the Bears in Chicago because there are major hurdles with stadium proposals in both Arlington Heights and Hammond, Indiana — the two sites on the Bears' short list for a new stadium.</p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-790000" exclusively on Arlington Heights. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/04/22/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-property-tax-relief-infrastructure-northwest-indiana" target="_blank" >megaprojects bill </a>that would allow the Bears to negotiate discounted property tax payments with local school districts is now before the Illinois Senate after passing the House. Major changes are needed to make property tax relief for suburban homeowners more than just a token break.</p><p>Pritzker said Monday he anticipates changes, and he expects the bill to pass both chambers and land on his desk before the Legislature adjourns its spring session May 31.</p><p>“The Bears have said publicly, and I think they said so last Friday, again, that they have now only two options — and that's the state of Indiana or Arlington Heights. We would like them to stay in the state of Illinois, and so I’m fighting hard to make sure they can do that,” Pritzker said.</p><p>When the NFL holds its quarterly meeting in Orlando Tuesday, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/18/bears-nfl-stadium-sites-arlington-heights-hammond-not-hammond-nfl-quarterly-meeting-orlando-tuesday" >Bears plan to reiterate</a> to the other 31 teams that the only two viable sites they are considering are Arlington Heights and Hammond — and nowhere else, a source told the Sun-Times Monday. The team has said it plans to decide between the two in late spring or early summer. </p><p>The governor reiterated that his “north star” is protecting Illinois taxpayers by making certain that no public money goes toward stadium construction.</p><p>It's important that “we are being fair with other businesses who want to come to Illinois or expand here — that we’re being fair in the allocation of support for a business expanding in that state while also protecting taxpayers across the state,” he said.</p><p>Reacting to Pritzker's remarks, Johnson's office released a statement saying, "For the past two years, the City has continued to advocate for a publicly owned stadium and has not supported the advancement of a privately owned stadium. The City’s proposal remains the only plan centered on public ownership alongside a funding mechanism that does not burden property taxpayers while keeping the Bears in Chicago."</p><p>In the three years since Johnson took office, the mayor and the governor have clashed over the migrant crisis, Chicago crime, leadership of the Democratic National Convention and the parade of tax increases and mandates that Johnson has imposed or attempted to impose on Chicago’s business community.</p><p>After a January 2025 run-in with the mayor over the governor’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cannabis/2025/01/06/johnson-pritzker-hemp-products-laws-marijunana-business-licenses-quinn-tabares-midway-airport" >stalled hemp regulations,</a> Pritzker complained the mayor and his team “don’t have good relationships in Springfield, in part, because they don’t do the outreach that’s necessary.”</p><p>The friction continued a few months later, when Pritzker threw cold water on the mayor’s demand for increased funding for the cash-strapped city and the Chicago Public Schools.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/05/14/mayor-brandon-johnson-no-cps-school-closings-re-election-bid-united-center-tax-break-sun-times-wbez-interview" >During an interview</a> with the Sun-Times and WBEZ last week, Johnson said he felt he had a “solid working relationship” with Pritzker. “We don't agree on everything. Why am I expected to agree with everyone on everything?” Johnson asked. "That's just not humanly possible. And when there's tension and friction, that's what makes us stronger. We have to push one another.”</p><p></p><p><i>Contributing: Pat Finley, Matt Trunfio from Springfield.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-330000" name="module-330000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Latest on the Bears stadium </h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/11/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana-what-to-know" ><b>Arlington Heights or Hammond</b></a>: The Bears no longer want to play in the smallest stadium in the NFL, so they’re on the hunt for a new place to play. entries.title: Trial nearing in case of remaining 'Broadview 6' ICE protesters, who may be labeled members of a 'mob'
entries.summary: <p>If the remaining members of the “Broadview Six” head to trial next week, federal prosecutors have already agreed not to slap them with labels like “rioters,”<b> </b>“domestic terrorists”<b> </b>or “Antifa members.”</p><p>But they might say they were part of a “mob.”</p><p>U.S. District Judge April Perry refused to bar the term Monday. She told defense attorneys the word is “fine, it is not a big deal.” And she said they’d be allowed to argue to jurors their own characterizations of the crowd that formed around an immigration agent’s vehicle<b> </b>Sept. 26.</p><p>But a hearing held in Perry’s courtroom Monday revolved around the larger question of whether prosecutors will try to hold the four demonstrators accountable at trial for their own actions — or the crowd’s. In fact, the judge pressed the feds on that very question minutes after she agreed they could say “mob.”</p><p>When a prosecutor said he had no intention of trying to convict the four based on the actions of others, she told him it “very much”<b> </b>sounded like he’d argued otherwise. She ultimately said she’d hold the feds to their word.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/29/broadview-ice-crime-chicago-trump-kat-abughezaleh" >Feds drop conspiracy charge against ‘Broadview Six’ ICE protesters, who still face trial for impeding officer</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The case is one of the most highly publicized prosecutions to result from last fall’s Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign. That’s because it <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/29/kat-abughazaleh-conspiracy-indictment-broadview-protests-donald-trump-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >began<b> </b>as a conspiracy case</a> against six people who protested outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility<b> </b>in suburban Broadview.</p><p>But the feds <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" target="_blank" >dropped charges against two</a> of the original six, and then they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/29/broadview-ice-crime-chicago-trump-kat-abughezaleh" target="_blank" >abandoned the conspiracy charge</a> altogether. Now, four people face one misdemeanor count each<b> </b>of forcibly impeding a federal agent.</p><p>Charged are former congressional candidate Kat<b> </b>Abughazaleh, Oak Park village trustee Brian<b> </b>Straw, 45th Ward Democratic committeeperson Michael<b> </b>Rabbitt<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andre<b> </b>Martin, who served as a member of Abughazaleh’s campaign staff.</p><p>The latest charging document in the case, filed April 29, does not offer specific allegations against the defendants. Generally, they’ve been accused of joining a larger group of protesters who surrounded an ICE agent’s vehicle and pushed, scratched and otherwise damaged it as it approached the facility in Broadview.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/03/12/chicago-midway-blitz-immigration-trump-kat-abughazaleh-sharp-joselyn-walsh-broadview-six" >Broadview 4? Feds drop conspiracy charges against 2 ICE protesters, including Dem who ended campaign</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Federal prosecutors raised eyebrows last week when, despite dropping the conspiracy charge, they argued in a brief that “all the actions by all the members of the mob were clearly foreseeable to each of them. They are all therefore responsible for [their fellow protesters’] conduct.”</p><p>“The government’s theory in this case has always been that the defendants were part of a mob that impeded, intimidated, and interfered with [the agent] on September 26, 2025, and … are therefore each accountable for the foreseeable acts of their joint venturers, charged or not,” prosecutors wrote in a filing Thursday.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorney William Hogan told the judge Monday, “we’re seeking to hold them accountable for the damage that was perpetrated or caused to the vehicle.”</p><p>But Perry told him, “you’re going to need some aiding and abetting [jury] instructions, and you didn’t propose them.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A crowd surrounds the federal agent’s vehicle on Sept. 26 outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Broadview.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The judge went on to clarify a defense argument for Hogan. She told him the defense hoped to stop his team from seeking the defendants’ convictions because someone else had pounded on the agent’s car.</p><p>“We’re not,” Hogan told the judge.</p><p>“That is very much like what your motions sounded like, and what you were saying earlier,” Perry replied.</p><p>Earlier in the hearing, Hogan also told the judge, “we’re not going to say that they’re guilty of impeding this agent because some other people in the crowd were saying ‘F the police.’”</p><p>Abughazaleh attorney Josh<b> </b>Herman<b> </b>replied, “can we get that in an order, please?”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" >Tracking every known federal prosecution in Chicago tied to Trump’s deportation blitz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The trial is set to begin May 26 and could last roughly two weeks. Perry said 90 potential jurors would be called to the Dirksen Federal Courthouse to possibly hear the case. The judge said she’s “very much hoping that jury selection doesn’t take days and days.”</p><p>But, she added, “I know it’s going to be challenging.”</p><p>She also agreed to review an unredacted transcript from grand jury proceedings in the case, at the urging of defense attorneys. It’s the same transcript she’d asked prosecutors to bring to a hearing late last month.</p><p>When that hearing began, prosecutors announced that they’d be abandoning the grand jury’s indictment and instead level misdemeanor charges in a separate charging document. Perry concluded at the time that she didn’t need to see the transcript, but the episode raised the suspicions of defense attorneys.</p><p>Finally, Perry on Monday rejected a request from defense attorneys that jurors be taken to Broadview so they could view the scene of the alleged crime. Not only would such a “field trip” be incredibly rare, she said, the “risk of something going wrong is massive.”</p><p>That’s because jurors would be in an uncontrolled, public place during a highly publicized trial.</p><p>But prosecutors had not objected to the outing,<b> </b>so Perry said she appreciated that the two sides had at least found something they could agree on.</p><p>That’s when Hogan clarified the feds’ position.</p><p>He said it was “more of a ‘we don’t care.’”</p>

entries.title: Brazilian’s quest to run on every Chicago street can continue despite visa scare
entries.summary: <p>When Joabe Barbosa set out to run on every street in Chicago, he didn't know how long he'd be allowed to stay in the United States.</p><p>Now, as the Roosevelt University graduate student prepares to complete his journey next month, he does so knowing Chicago will remain home.</p><p>Two weeks ago, Barbosa found out he would be able to stay through 2028 after Roosevelt University arranged for him to teach undergraduate classes while continuing coursework. That followed an outpouring of support from the thousands of followers who tracked his journey through Chicago's streets.</p><p>And it came with a few proposals.</p><p>While his future in Chicago remained uncertain, Barbosa said his inboxes were flooded with close to 500 marriage proposals and several offers for his adoption.</p><p>But his mom refused, he said, laughing.</p><p>"The people of Chicago were definitely very helpful in providing me so many opportunities. And just knowing that, if it didn't work out, I had so many people to depend on," Barbosa said.</p><p>Barbosa, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/04/01/brazilian-student-who-is-nearly-done-running-on-every-street-in-chicago-faces-departure-as-visa-expires" >a native Brazilian who grew up in London</a>, moved to Chicago in 2022 on an F-1 visa to pursue a doctorate degree in clinical psychology at Roosevelt University. But after going unmatched for an internship during his final year, Barbosa faced the possibility of being forced to return to Brazil. </p><p>Since then, Barbosa has continued to run through the streets of Chicago for more than 400 days, gaining more than 50,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. </p><p>"I didn't count, but I probably have someone from every one of the Chicago neighborhoods that I could probably stay with for a year for free," he said.</p><p>Barbosa said the university gave him financial support, offsetting the burden on his family so he could continue his studies. As an international student, he said his family has taken on debt to help him cover the cost of his education.</p><p></p><p>On June 14, he will make his final run down Michigan Avenue from Oak Street to Ida B. Wells Drive. </p><p>Despite not being American, Barbosa said Chicago has become his home. </p><p>"Truly, after this last lap, it'll show how much community and how much love there is for people here and how much love there is for people that truly embrace Chicago," he said. </p>

entries.title: Man stalked ex-husband’s new partner before targeting him in deadly Edgewater shooting, court records allege
entries.summary: <p>Court records show Ammar Houssamo had a long history of stalking his ex-husband’s new partner, Nick Calzaretta.</p><p>It started in August 2023, when Houssamo allegedly sent a message to Calzaretta on a dating app asking him to be “friends with benefits,” and soon escalated, the records show.</p><p>In a series of court filings, Calzaretta said Houssamo’s actions forced him to quit his job and made him worried about leaving home, fearing what his alleged stalker “would do next.” </p><p>Those fears weren’t unfounded, according to officials.</p><p>Cook County prosecutors say Houssamo tracked Calzaretta down as he was walking his dog Thursday morning in Edgewater. As Calzaretta screamed out “leave me alone,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/15/dog-walker-fatally-shot-trying-fleeing-gunman-who-then-turned-gun-on-self-in-edgewater-police" target="_blank" >Houssamo fatally shot him</a> before turning the gun on himself, according to a police report.</p><p>Houssamo, 53, had previously referenced suicide while speaking to Calzaretta and his ex-husband, court records show. But Houssamo survived a self-inflicted gunshot wound last week, and he’s now <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/16/rogers-park-man-charged-in-fatal-edgewater-shooting" target="_blank" >charged with first-degree murder</a> and illegal gun possession in the jarring attack in the 1400 block of West Thome Avenue.</p><p>The shooting came two years after Cook County Judge Donald D. Panarese Jr. vacated a protective order keeping Houssamo from contacting or interacting with Calzaretta or his then-husband.</p><p>Calzaretta’s younger brother, Russell, said the family is now questioning how Houssamo got the guns recovered by police, and why the protective order was lifted. He said the system failed his brother, as it has failed many others before.</p><p>“It’s disheartening to know there were so many red flags, and they weren't taken seriously,” Russell Calzaretta told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>“A piece of paper won't protect him from bullets, but it’s all that we have in our justice system. To know Nick wasn't protected by the people who are supposed to have our best interest at heart, it makes me wonder how many more people will be in the same situation, how many families will have to go through the same thing.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-610000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Nick Calzaretta was killed in a shooting last week while walking his dog in Edgewater. His partner’s ex-husband, Ammar Houssamo, was charged in the attack after also shooting himself, officials said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Calzaretta, 37, was pronounced dead at Presence St. Francis Hospital in Evanston. Houssamo was hospitalized in critical condition and remained there, though he’s expected to appear at a detention hearing Tuesday, court records show.</p><p>Calzaretta was granted an emergency protective order against Houssamo in September 2023, according to court documents. In an amended petition filed a month later, Calzaretta said he had been “avoiding his routine social activities” and “obsessively thinking about what [Houssamo] would do next.”</p><p>Houssamo was repeatedly messaging him on social media and had sent at least 25 of Calzaretta’s co-workers emails about his sex life, Calzaretta alleged. It led Calzaretta to resign a short time later.</p><p>At the time, Calzaretta was dating Houssamo's husband following the married couple’s separation months earlier, according to a lawsuit.</p><p>About a week after Houssamo learned Calzaretta was in a relationship with his estranged husband, he messaged Calzaretta on a dating website asking him to be “friends with benefits,” records show. Houssamo told his estranged husband about the message, saying he may start the divorce process and that it “‘it might kill me or I may kill myself soon after.”</p><p>Houssamo filed for divorce just days after Calzaretta’s order of protection was granted, records show. The court also ordered Houssamo to stay away from his ex.</p><p>The order was extended on Oct. 2, 2023, the same day Calzaretta said he rushed back inside his apartment when he saw Houssamo approaching the building. It was weeks after Houssamo sent him messages that again mentioned suicide and included explicit details of his prior relationship, Calzaretta alleged in court records.</p><p>In January 2024, Calzaretta filed a petition saying Houssamo had violated the order by posting videos about him on social media, according to court records. Houssamo was arrested and charged but was ultimately found not guilty of a violation.</p><p>Calzaretta attempted to extend the protective order, but it was dissolved in April 2024 without explanation in the court docket.</p><p>In August of that year, Houssamo sued Calzaretta for $75,000, alleging he intentionally inflicted emotional damage with the allegations made in his petition for the protective order. Houssamo argued that he never sent the emails to Calzaretta’s co-workers that led to Calzaretta’s resignation.</p><p>Houssamo and his ex-husband’s divorce proceedings wrapped up in January 2025, six months later, with a closing stipulation from the judge that Houssamo remove a post he made on Facebook about his ex-husband the day prior, according to court records.</p><p>Houssamo’s lawsuit against Calzaretta was dismissed last November, records show.</p><p>Russell said he hopes his brother’s death leads to reform around protective orders and gun control.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-senate/2026/02/05/state-senate-republicans-legislative-package-domestic-violence" target="_blank" ><u>Legislation introduced</u> in Springfield</a> earlier this year would create higher penalties for violating protective court orders and make violating an order a felony, as opposed to a misdemeanor. The bills were brought in response to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/02/02/amazon-ring-cameras-illinois-domestic-violence-survivors-attorney-general-kwame-raoul" target="_blank" >140% rise in domestic violence deaths</a> since 2022.</p><p>“We need reform, and it needs to be harder for people to have guns, because my brother is gone and it’s not fair,” Russell said. “It doesn't have to be this way. … I don't want my brother to be a statistic because he was so much more than that.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: Race is on for Chicago’s first fully elected school board
entries.summary: <p>LaPamela Williams was one of dozens who lined up early Monday morning to submit the signatures she gathered to run for a seat on what will soon be Chicago’s fully elected school board.</p><p>Williams, a realtor, is running to represent subdistrict 5A on the city’s West Side. She hoped being among the first to file nomination petitions with city officials would get her better placement on November’s ballot.</p><p>It's her first time running for office. Already, she said, the signature-gathering process has been “eye opening” because it allowed her to gauge which issues matter the most to her would-be constituents. Some of her own priorities include increasing financial literacy instruction and finding ways to keep students from missing too much school.</p><p>“If I am able to get onto the board I can take that and look for practical solutions for the community,” Williams said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>LaPamela Williams is running to represent a West Side subdistrict on the Chicago School Board. Increasing financial literacy instruction and curbing chronic absenteeism are top priorities for her as a candidate.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Williams was among 50 people, including prospective school board candidates, incumbents and supporters, who waited outside the Chicago Voter Supersite in the Loop for the doors to open at 9 a.m. As they filed their petitions, it marked the official start of this year’s Chicago School Board races.</p><p>Many candidates said they planned to focus on increasing students’ reading and math scores, ensuring the board operates independently and improving the district’s financial transparency as part of their campaigns.</p><p>Whoever is elected will also have to tackle the district’s ongoing financial troubles, declining enrollment and federal probes by the Trump administration. Federal agencies have threatened to withhold funding for the district and launched investigations into CPS for its plan to improve academic outcomes for Black students and its policy that allows transgender students to use the bathroom that aligns with their gender identity.</p><p>The city held its first school board elections in 2024 but only 10 seats were up for grabs that year. This year, all 20 seats as well as the citywide board president position will be decided by voters.</p><p>Candidates for school board are required to submit at least 500 signatures, while those running for board president need at least 2,500. They have until May 26 to file their petitions. Each candidate in line Monday morning presented stacks of paper to election officials to confirm they had enough signatures.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong regrets vulgar, viral response to heckler, won’t ‘let stuff like that fly’
entries.summary: <p>Pete Crow-Armstrong knows that he should have known better.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ star center fielder wasn’t talking about his latest highlight-reel catch or clutch homer Monday at Wrigley Field. Instead, he found himself discussing his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/17/crosstown-rivalry-gets-spicy-thanks-to-pete-crow-armstrong-and-fan" >vulgar retort to a heckling fan</a> during Sunday’s loss to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> after it went viral on social media.</p><p>“I’m just bummed out about the word choice and that a bunch of little kids probably find their way to social media and see that, as well,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I am intense on the field, and in a moment like that, I just let it get away from me a little bit. Poor word choice.”</p><p>Those specifics are easy enough to find. Earmuffs, kids.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">PCA was not too happy with Sox fans today! <a href="https://twitter.com/barstoolchicago?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@barstoolchicago</a> <a href="https://t.co/oVHHAdQQV2">pic.twitter.com/oVHHAdQQV2</a></p>— Barstool Sports (@barstoolsports) <a href="https://twitter.com/barstoolsports/status/2056173496300871903?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><p>Crow-Armstrong’s comeback to a female White Sox fan contained derogatory language that shouldn’t be directed at any woman. That’s what stirred up the remorse the 2025 All Star was feeling.</p><p>“I don’t think that any of the women in my life would ever think that I would use those kinds of words regularly, especially referring to them,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I think everybody that knows me knows that’s something that came out specifically with being directly related to baseball in that situation.</p><p>“That is not something I pride myself on being about, calling people names like that. But most importantly, the women in my life know I don’t love that choice of word.”</p><p>Hecklers are an occupational hazard for pro ballplayers. It seemed Crow-Armstrong was White Sox fans’ top target during the weekend’s Crosstown series on the South Side, no surprise as he’s the Cubs’ highest profile player.</p><p>“That’s probably been the case dating back to the earliest days of this game,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I’m sure people found ways to get under our skin and whatnot. It’s just a shame that I let that one person do that.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Pete Crow-Armstrong regrets his choice of words during an altercation with a fan at the <a href="https://twitter.com/hashtag/Cubs?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#Cubs</a> & <a href="https://twitter.com/hashtag/WhiteSox?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#WhiteSox</a> Crosstown Classic finale <br><br>More from PCA: <a href="https://t.co/ETAlkI4xyq">https://t.co/ETAlkI4xyq</a> <a href="https://t.co/vizLY5BlOI">pic.twitter.com/vizLY5BlOI</a></p>— GNSportsTV (@GNSportsTV) <a href="https://twitter.com/GNSportsTV/status/2056490718437277701?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Talk a day later centered on the responsibility players have to control their reactions, especially important in the age of camera phones and social media.</p><p>“I think every player can say that [they’ve been frustrated by interactions with fans],” Cubs manager Craig Counsell, a former player himself, said. “Sometimes it’s fun, and sometimes it’s funny, actually. Sometimes it’s hurtful, and that happens a lot, too. But we have a standard to uphold that goes along with all the good stuff that we get to experience.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong did not specifically apologize for firing back at the heckling fan, even if he wasn’t happy with how he did it.</p><p>Every Cubs fan knows he’s not shy about wearing his emotions on his sleeve, though his fiery outbursts are typically reserved for equipment like bats and helmets.</p><p>More often, the Cubs reap the rewards of Crow-Armstrong’s high-energy, emotional approach. He can fire up his teammates with his play on the field like few players around the sport can.</p><p>“Pete, he’s an emotional player. … I think that’s a good thing,” Counsell said. “It’ll improve, and it’ll be pointed in the right direction better as he gains experience. But it’s important for him, and he needs it. And we love it. We love a lot of it. But there’s also going to be learning moments from it.”</p><p>Much like Crow-Armstrong has no intention of easing off the gas when it comes to his on-field play, he’s not planning to shrink from future run-ins — though he’s going to approach it with a more thoughtful vocabulary.</p><p>“I don’t want to let [cameras being on me like Sunday] deter me from the competitiveness that I feel out on the field,” he said. “Channeling it in a different way would be my next task.</p><p>“But I’m not always going to let stuff like that fly, either. It’s just about being a little more respectful and killing somebody with kindness instead of matching their level of intent.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module entries.title: White Sox mashing their way to respectability behind Mune, Montgomery and Miguel
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> have found some unlikely heroes while jumping to their best start in five years.</p><p>There was Derek Hill, the fourth outfielder-turned-<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/12/derek-hill-pinch-hit-homer-diving-catch-white-sox-royals-bobby-witt-will-venable-seranthony-dominguez-bryan-hudson" target="_blank" ><u>pinch-hit-home run specialist</u></a>, setting down the division-rival Royals. There was Tristan Peters, the ex-Saluki and ex-Savannah Banana, crushing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/white-sox-edgar-quero-tristan-peters-upstage-cubs-everyone-else-in-wild-9-8-bash" target="_blank" ><u>a tie-breaking homer</u></a> against the hated Cubs. And just in the nick of time, there was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/17/edgar-quero-white-sox-rally-past-cubs-to-take-crosstown-series" target="_blank" ><u>Edgar Quero</u></a> making up for his woeful first two months of the year with a walk-off blast that’ll play in Crosstown highlight reels for generations to come.</p><p>While anything seems possible in mid-May for a rebuilding squad that’s finally looking competitive, those three names probably aren’t joining the household variety in Chicago anytime soon — even if the Sox can take another step from mediocre in the wide-open American League Central.</p><p>But there’s no question about the three M’s at the heart of the batting order whose consistent production has all of baseball reconsidering what the Sox might be able to accomplish in Year Three of general manager Chris Getz’s organizational overhaul: Munetaka Murakami, Colson Montgomery and Miguel Vargas.</p><p>The high-powered infield triumvirate had accounted for nearly two-thirds of the Sox’ eye-popping 66 homers entering play Monday, tied for second-most in Major League Baseball, with Murakami’s 17 leading the American League. The Sox led MLB in the 30 days leading up to their six-game West Coast road trip in homers (46) and OPS (.817).</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Colson Montgomery joins in on the fun! 🤩 <a href="https://t.co/oAUECPrScn">pic.twitter.com/oAUECPrScn</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2055798929581592871?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>It’s been a long path for the team’s offseason splurge from Japan, who has left 29 other teams shaking their heads after passing on his meager free-agent market.</p><p>The journeys have been just as long for Montgomery, who has shouldered the hopes of the rebuild since being drafted in 2021, and Vargas, who looked downright miserable after arriving from the high-flying Dodgers in the middle of the Sox’ historically bad 2024 season.</p><p>Now the trio are regularly sharing sushi-eating dugout celebrations while taking pressure off each other and a suddenly potent lineup in a season that’s actually carrying some marginal expectations.</p><p>“It just shows what this lineup is capable of doing,” Montgomery said ahead of the Sox’ rubber-match win against the Cubs before heading to Seattle. “It just takes a lot of pressure off a lot of us. We have runners on base, I’m on deck and I’m like, ‘Vargas, he draws a lot of walks.’ You get up to bat and I need to try to do something, but then he hits a three-run homer and it’s like, ‘Alright, now we are rolling.’ It takes the pressure off of everything.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tie ballgame courtesy of Miguel Vargas! <a href="https://t.co/D1NZOfXbn4">pic.twitter.com/D1NZOfXbn4</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2056101401856459098?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 17, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Montgomery has built on his impressive rookie campaign to a .238/.335/.524 start with 13 homers and 31 RBI. The shortstop would be the Sox’ story of the year if not for the thunderous debut from Murakami (.235/.372/.562), not that Montgomery’s complaining.</p><p>“Last year [I] didn't really have much of a guy I could gauge off how I might get pitched,” he said. “Having a guy up here who's also a left-handed bat and has power, it's one of those things where I'm kind of getting questions to a test.”</p><p>Flying under the radar but perhaps not for much longer has been the third baseman Vargas, who’s hitting .247/.374/.506 with 11 homers and 29 RBI.</p><p>“He's shown glimpses of it and I feel like now his work and preparation is kind of showing off,” Montgomery said. “Your preparation, your process — if you command that, in our heads, it's like, we're going to have success. He's been banging and it's been fun to watch.”</p><p>The homer-happy Sox have banged out nearly 52% of their runs via the long ball, according to Baseball Prospectus, but their recent run is more reliant on demeanor than distance, according to manager Will Venable.</p><p>“They’ve just continued to play all nine innings, every single pitch. It’s something [hitting coach Derek] Shomon talks about in the hitters’ meetings,” Venable said. “They have the energy for it and they just continue to put out a lot of energy on a daily basis.”</p><p></p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Rush University Medical Center nurses celebrate successful vote to unionize
entries.summary: <p>When it became clear Monday that Rush University Medical Center nurses had secured enough votes for union representation, two of Olivia Bouchard’s co-workers ran up and gave her a hug.</p><p>“You just won your union,” one of the women said to a beaming Bouchard, who helped organize the nurses.</p><p>They were in a jubilant crowd of about 50 nurses gathered Monday at the Billy Goat Tavern in the West Loop for a watch party as the National Labor Relations Board tallied the union election votes.</p><p>Within two hours of the tally, the nurses had reached enough votes in favor of being represented by the National Nurses Organizing Committee, an affiliate of the larger National Nurses United. The final count saw 77% of nurses vote in support — a number the group chanted in celebration.</p><p>“We are united in our front,” said Bouchard, a nurse in the hospital’s labor and delivery unit. “And once you get a big group of powerful — mostly women — together, we make moves pretty fast.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure
